title: Hold, Sell or Refinance: One Question With Three Doors
summary: Hold, sell and refinance are three answers to one question: where should the equity in this building be working now? This lesson teaches return on equity in place, the three doors and what each costs, how to think about the cycle without pretending to time it, and the options in between.
body:
Hold, sell and refinance are not three separate decisions. They are three answers to one question: is the equity now sitting in this building earning enough, after tax and after risk, to justify leaving it there?

Recall

Q. How do you separate the operating gain from the market gain in a change in value?

A. Apply last period's capitalisation rate to this period's net operating income. The change at a constant rate is what operations earned; the remainder is the effect of the cap rate moving.

Q. What is economic occupancy?

A. Rent actually collected as a share of potential rent. It falls with concessions, discounts and arrears even when every unit is physically occupied.

Q. What is the difference between substantial and final completion?

A. Substantial completion is the point at which the work is usable for its intended purpose, with only minor items outstanding. Final completion comes when the punch list, documents and closeout obligations are all finished. The contract defines both.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the most valuable decisions in an owner's career often happen after the building is finished. A developer who never asks the question simply holds by default, and default is a decision with no analysis behind it. A developer who sells too eagerly pays transaction costs and tax again and again, and loses compounding. Elias joins me this week because the after-tax answer is frequently different from the pre-tax one, and the difference is where wealth is kept or lost.

Equity in place, not equity invested

In plain English: what matters is the money you could take out of the building today, not the money you once put in.

The professional framing is return on equity in place. Equity in place is the market value of the building, less the debt, less what it would cost to sell, and, for a fair comparison, less the tax that a sale would trigger. Divide the building's annual cash flow after debt service and reserves by that figure, and you have the return the equity is actually earning now.

A worked example with hypothetical round numbers. You invested 6,000,000 dollars of equity five years ago. The building is now worth 30,000,000 dollars, with 15,000,000 dollars of debt. Cash flow after debt service and reserves is 700,000 dollars a year. On the original 6,000,000 dollars, that looks like an 11.7 percent return. But the equity in place, before costs and tax, is 15,000,000 dollars, and on that the return is only 4.7 percent. Success has quietly lowered your return, because value rose faster than income. That is the moment to ask the question.

Say that out loud now.

Success lowers the return on equity in place. That is when I ask whether the equity should move.

The three doors

Hold. Keep the building and its debt. You keep the cash flow, the future growth and the risk, and you pay no transaction cost and trigger no sale tax. Holding is right when the return on equity in place, adjusted for risk, beats what the same equity could earn elsewhere.

Sell. Realise the value. You pay selling costs and, in most systems, tax on the gain, and you are left with cash to redeploy. Selling is right when the market is paying more than the building is worth to you, when the building needs capital you do not want to spend, or when concentration risk on your balance sheet is too high.

Refinance. Replace the existing loan with a larger one and take cash out, keeping the building. In many systems borrowed money is not taxable income when received, which is why refinancing is attractive; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. But a larger loan means larger debt service, a lower debt service coverage ratio and more risk. Refinancing is right when the cash can earn more elsewhere than the cost of the new debt, and the building can carry the debt through a downturn.

The doors in between

The choice is rarely all or nothing. A partial sale, selling a share of the building to a partner, releases equity and shares risk while you keep control and perhaps a fee for managing it. A recapitalisation replaces some or all of your existing investors or lenders with new ones on new terms. A supplemental loan, where a lender permits it, adds a smaller second loan without disturbing the first. Each has its own cost, tax treatment and governance. Professional sign-off required: lawyer and tax adviser on any partial sale or recapitalisation.

Timing the cycle without pretending to

Nobody reliably sells at the top. What disciplined owners do instead is decide in advance what would make them act. They set triggers: if the cap rate on comparable sales falls below a chosen level, run the sale analysis; if the loan is within 24 months of maturity, start the refinance work; if one asset exceeds a set share of net worth, consider a partial sale. Triggers turn a market mood into a written rule. The numbers in a trigger are your choice, not a standard.

A second worked example. Your loan matures in 18 months. Rates have risen, and at today's rate the building's NOI supports a new loan of only 13,000,000 dollars, against the 15,000,000 dollars you owe. That gap of 2,000,000 dollars is the refinance problem, and it is far easier to solve 18 months out, with time to raise equity, negotiate an extension or sell, than in the final 90 days. Maturity is a cycle risk you can see coming; the control is to start early.

Notice what the example does to the three doors. With a refinance gap of 2,000,000 dollars, a full cash-out refinance is off the table entirely; the realistic choices become a smaller refinance with an equity paydown, an extension, a partial sale or a full sale. The cycle did not tell you which door to choose. It closed one of them. That is the honest way to think about timing: not as a forecast of the top, but as a set of doors that open and close as rates, cap rates and maturities move.

How the best do it

The most disciplined owners run a hold, sell and refinance analysis on every asset once a year, whether or not anyone is offering to buy. They compare the internal rate of return, IRR, of holding from today forward, on today's value as the starting investment, with the after-tax return of redeploying the equity. A small developer can copy that with one page per building: equity in place after cost and tax, return on it, and the alternative.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: a sale usually triggers tax on the gain and may recapture depreciation previously claimed, while borrowing usually does not; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: a cash-out refinance may bring new guarantees or recourse. Banking: start refinance discussions well before maturity, when you have choices. Governance: partner agreements often require consent for a sale or a new loan. Estate: in some systems, holding until death changes how the gain is taxed, so the estate plan belongs in the analysis. Exit: every door is an exit choice; holding is choosing to exit later.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is holding by default, with no comparison made, until a loan maturity or a market turn forces a decision on the worst terms. The control is an annual written hold, sell and refinance analysis, plus triggers set in advance.

The beginner's mistake

Measuring return on the original equity instead of the equity in place. The original number flatters every successful building and hides the cost of leaving equity where it is.

Callback

In Week 45, Nadia and Priya taught exit financing: refinance, take-out, bridge loans and maturity gaps. That lesson was about leaving the construction loan. This week the same tools reappear at the far end of ownership, and the maturity gap is the same animal: debt due on a date, and a market that may not be there to repay it.

Recap

Hold, sell and refinance answer one question: should the equity in place stay? Measure return on equity in place, after cost and tax. Hold keeps growth and risk; sell pays cost and tax for liquidity; refinance borrows cash at the price of more risk. Use partial sales and triggers rather than pretending to time the cycle.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: Olympia and York, and long buildings financed on short money.
checklist: I calculate return on equity in place for each building, after selling costs and tax.
I run a written hold, sell and refinance analysis on every asset each year.
I compare the hold return from today with the after-tax redeployment return.
I know each loan's maturity date and start refinance work at least 18 to 24 months out.
I have written triggers for when to run a sale or refinance analysis.
I consider partial sales and recapitalisations, not only all-or-nothing choices.
I know which partner consents a sale or new loan requires.
I include the estate plan in any long-hold decision.
head: Field checklist
speak: Hold, sell and refinance are three answers to one question: should the equity now in this building stay there? I measure return on equity in place: market value less debt, selling costs and the tax a sale would trigger, compared with cash flow after debt and reserves. In my hypothetical example, 700,000 dollars of cash flow looks like 11.7 percent on the original 6,000,000 dollars, but only 4.7 percent on 15,000,000 dollars of equity in place. Success lowered the return. Holding keeps growth and risk without cost or tax. Selling pays cost and usually tax for cash to redeploy. Refinancing borrows cash out, often untaxed when received, at the price of higher debt service and risk. There are doors in between: partial sales and recapitalisations. I do not pretend to time the cycle. I set triggers in advance, start refinancing well before maturity, and run the analysis on every asset every year.
terms: Return on equity in place — annual cash flow after debt service and reserves divided by the equity that could be taken out of the building today.
Hold-sell analysis — a periodic comparison of the return from holding an asset from today forward with the after-tax return from selling and redeploying.
Recapitalisation — replacing some or all of a property's investors or lenders with new capital on new terms.

hostile.q: Your building has tripled in value. Why are you still holding it?
hostile.a: Because on this year's analysis, the hold return on equity in place, after the tax a sale would trigger, is still above what I can earn redeploying it at the same risk. Here is the one-page comparison: equity in place after cost and tax, return on it, and the alternative. If comparable sales cap rates fall below my trigger, or the loan comes within two years of maturity, I re-run it. I am holding by choice, not by default.

title: Olympia and York: Long Buildings on Short Money
summary: Olympia and York, the Reichmann family's Toronto-based developer, built some of the largest office projects of the 1980s, including Canary Wharf in London. Heavy reliance on short-term borrowing met a falling property market, refinancing failed, and in May 1992 the company sought creditor protection while Canary Wharf entered administration. Seven steps show why maturity, not quality, decided the outcome.
body:
Olympia and York owned remarkable buildings and still failed, because the debt behind them came due before the market would refinance it. When the hold decision depends on rolling short money, the lender, not the owner, decides when you sell.

Recall

Q. What is return on equity in place?

A. Annual cash flow after debt service and reserves divided by the equity that could be taken out of the building today, after debt, selling costs and, for a fair comparison, tax.

Q. Why should a reserve that funds debt service be reported as a runway in months?

A. Because a reserve being drawn every month is a countdown, not a cushion. The runway shows how long the plan has before the money runs out.

Q. What does an integrated systems test prove at closeout?

A. That building systems work correctly together, for example that a fire alarm signal shuts down the right air handlers and releases the right doors, after each system has passed its own functional test.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me because this is the purest refinance failure on record in our field: an owner with high-quality assets, a strong reputation and a long-term view, whose debt had a short-term view. For a small developer the scale is irrelevant. The mechanism is not. If your hold depends on refinancing on a date, you have given the market a vote on your hold decision.

I will state only well-documented facts: the company, its flagship projects, the downturn of the early 1990s, its reliance on short-term borrowing and the May 1992 filings. Where I describe dynamics or use numbers, they are general or hypothetical.

1. Timeline

Olympia and York, controlled by the Reichmann family and based in Toronto, grew in the 1970s and 1980s into one of the largest commercial property developers in the world, with major office holdings in Toronto and New York, including the World Financial Center in Lower Manhattan. In the late 1980s it committed to Canary Wharf, a vast office development in London's Docklands, at a time when the area had weak transport links. Property markets in London, New York and Toronto weakened sharply around 1990 and 1991. The company relied in part on short-term borrowing, including commercial paper, which is unsecured short-term debt sold to investors and rolled over continually. As confidence fell, rolling that debt became harder. In May 1992 Olympia and York sought protection from creditors in Canada under the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act, and the Canary Wharf companies were placed in administration in the United Kingdom the same month.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Building a very large speculative project in a location whose value depended on transport that did not yet exist. Financing long-lived assets partly with short-dated debt that had to be replaced again and again. And concentrating a great share of the group's fortunes in that one project at the moment markets turned.

3. Assumptions

The assumptions were that credit would always be available to a borrower of this reputation, that tenants would follow the buildings, and that the transport link would arrive in time to support leasing. Each rested on the belief that time was on the owner's side. Short-term debt is precisely a bet that time is not needed.

4. Incentives

Short-term borrowing was cheaper than long-term borrowing for much of the period, which rewards using it. A strong reputation reduced lenders' scrutiny. A developer with a record of contrarian success had every reason to trust that it would be proved right again. Each incentive pushed toward more short money and more concentration.

Say that out loud now.

Cheap short debt on a long building is a bet that I will never need time. Buildings always need time.

5. Warning signs ignored

Leasing at the new project ran slower than a project of that size needed. Rents and values were falling in the group's home markets at the same time, which removed the option of selling elsewhere to fund the shortfall. And the cost of rolling short debt rises before it disappears; a rising spread on renewal is a lender saying it is losing confidence.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return came when lenders would no longer roll the short-term debt and the assets could not be sold quickly at prices that covered it. Once the refinancing door closed in a falling market, the hold decision had been made by the creditors.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a maturity mismatch: long-dated, slow-to-stabilise assets financed partly with short-dated debt, concentrated in one market cycle. The buildings were not the problem. The calendar was.

Roman's view: the maturity ladder

Here is the small-deal version, with hypothetical round numbers. You own three buildings, each with a 10,000,000 dollar loan. If all three mature in the same year, you need 30,000,000 dollars of refinancing in one market. If they mature in years three, five and seven, you need 10,000,000 dollars at a time, in three different markets, and a bad year affects one loan, not all of them. That spread is called a maturity ladder.

The second test is the refinance stress. For each loan, ask what NOI must be at maturity, at a higher rate and a higher cap rate, for a new lender to refinance the full balance. Suppose a building earns NOI of 1,000,000 dollars and owes 15,000,000 dollars. At a new loan rate of 7 percent on interest-only terms and a lender requirement of debt service coverage of 1.25, the maximum loan is NOI divided by 1.25, which is 800,000 dollars of interest, divided by 0.07, which is about 11,400,000 dollars. The gap is 3,600,000 dollars. If you see that gap two years out, it is a plan. If you see it in the last month, it is a crisis.

What a small developer copies

Match the term of the debt to the time the asset needs, and leave slack for delay. Ladder maturities so that no single year carries all your refinancing. Watch the spread at which lenders renew; a widening spread is a warning before a refusal. And start every refinance at least eighteen months before maturity, while you still have the option to extend, inject equity or sell on your own terms. Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on any extension or forbearance agreement.

One more habit belongs here, and it is about concentration rather than maturity. Olympia and York could not sell its home-market buildings to save the new project, because every market it owned fell together. A small developer with three buildings in one city faces the same correlation. When you hold, ask what you could sell quickly if one loan needed paying down, and at what discount. If the honest answer is nothing, your hold decision depends on the refinance market alone.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a maturity mismatch: holding an asset whose income needs years to arrive on debt that must be replaced before then. The control is matched term, a laddered maturity profile, a refinance stress test on each loan and an early start.

The beginner's mistake

Choosing the cheapest debt without asking when it comes due. The rate is visible on day one. The maturity is visible on the worst day.

Callback

In Week 46, Ford and Roman ran the first finance post-mortem: leverage spirals, maturity walls and guarantee calls. Olympia and York is the maturity wall at its largest. The lesson is identical at any size: the date the debt is due is a risk you choose when you sign.

Recap

A developer with outstanding buildings failed because short-term debt behind long-term assets could not be refinanced in a falling market. Leasing was slow, home markets fell together, and lenders stopped rolling the debt. In May 1992 the company sought creditor protection and Canary Wharf entered administration.

Rule 127: Never let the debt decide your hold; match loan term to the time the asset needs, ladder maturities, stress-test every refinance and start at least eighteen months before maturity.

Next: Roman on The Money: what each door, hold, sell or refinance, does to return and risk.
checklist: I match each loan's term to the time the asset needs, with slack for delay.
I ladder maturities so no single year carries most of my refinancing.
I run a refinance stress test on each loan at higher rates and cap rates.
I calculate the refinance gap for every loan at least two years out.
I track the spread at which lenders renew as an early warning.
I start refinancing at least eighteen months before maturity.
I avoid concentrating most of my equity in one market cycle.
head: Field checklist
speak: Olympia and York, the Reichmann family's Toronto-based developer, owned some of the finest office buildings of the 1980s, including the World Financial Center in New York, and committed to Canary Wharf in London's Docklands. Part of its financing was short-term debt, including commercial paper, which had to be rolled over continually. When property markets in London, New York and Toronto fell around 1990 and 1991, leasing slowed and lenders lost confidence. Rolling the debt became impossible, and in May 1992 the company sought creditor protection in Canada while Canary Wharf entered administration in Britain. The buildings were not the problem. The root cause was a maturity mismatch: long assets on short money, concentrated in one cycle. Rule 127: never let the debt decide my hold. I match term to the time the asset needs, ladder maturities, stress-test every refinance and start at least eighteen months before maturity.
terms: Maturity mismatch — financing a long-lived asset with debt that must be repaid or replaced before the asset's income can support it.
Commercial paper — unsecured short-term debt sold to investors and repeatedly rolled over, cheap in good markets and unavailable in bad ones.
Maturity ladder — spreading loan maturities across different years so that no single market carries all the refinancing.

hostile.q: Your loan matures in 14 months and our sizing shows a 3,000,000 dollar shortfall at today's rates. What is your plan?
hostile.a: I have three options in progress, and I will give you a written plan within two weeks. First, a 12 to 24 month extension with a paydown from cash flow and a rate step, which I would like to discuss with you now. Second, a partner equity injection, with terms in draft. Third, a sale of a minority interest. I started this work early so that I would have options, not because I expect you to carry the gap.

rule: Rule 127: Never let the debt decide your hold; match loan term to the time the asset needs, ladder maturities, stress-test every refinance and start at least eighteen months before maturity.

title: What Each Door Does to Return and Risk
summary: Selling, refinancing and holding change cash flow, risk and after-tax wealth in different directions. This lesson prices each door's effect on cash flow, debt service coverage, loan to value and the use of the released cash, and closes with Warrick's Wealth Ledger.
body:
Every door raises one thing and lowers another. Selling raises certainty and lowers growth; refinancing raises cash and lowers safety; holding keeps growth and keeps risk. The money is in knowing which trade you are making.

Recall

Q. What is a maturity mismatch?

A. Financing a long-lived asset with debt that must be repaid or replaced before the asset's income can support it.

Q. At a 5 percent cap rate, what is the value multiplier?

A. Twenty. Each recurring dollar of NOI is worth 20 dollars of value.

Q. What is a latent defect?

A. A defect in the work that could not be discovered by reasonable inspection at completion and appears later. Who bears it, and for how long, depends on the contract and the law.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a lender sees each door as a change in risk to its loan. An investor sees it as a change in return. You need to see both, because you are the one who lives with the result. This lesson is the arithmetic of each door. All numbers are hypothetical round figures. Tomorrow Elias teaches the tax rules that apply to them.

The base case

A stabilised building earns NOI of 1,500,000 dollars and is worth 30,000,000 dollars at a 5 percent cap rate. It carries a loan of 15,000,000 dollars at 5 percent interest only, so debt service is 750,000 dollars, and the reserve contribution is 50,000 dollars. Cash flow after debt service and reserves is 700,000 dollars. Loan to value is 50 percent. Debt service coverage ratio, DSCR, which is NOI divided by annual debt service, is 2.0.

Door one: refinance

A new lender offers 60 percent of value, 18,000,000 dollars, at 6 percent interest only. Costs, including fees and the cost of breaking the old loan, total 300,000 dollars. A cost of breaking the old loan early is often set by a prepayment penalty: a charge in the loan agreement for repaying before maturity. Its form and size are commercial terms in each loan; read your own.

Cash out: 18,000,000 minus 15,000,000 minus 300,000, which is 2,700,000 dollars. New debt service: 6 percent of 18,000,000, which is 1,080,000 dollars. New cash flow after reserves: 1,500,000 minus 1,080,000 minus 50,000, which is 370,000 dollars, down from 700,000. New DSCR: 1,500,000 divided by 1,080,000, which is about 1.39. Loan to value: 60 percent.

So the refinance swaps 330,000 dollars a year of cash flow for 2,700,000 dollars today. That trade pays only if the 2,700,000 dollars earns more than about 12 percent a year elsewhere, because 330,000 divided by 2,700,000 is 12.2 percent. The new debt costs 6 percent on the margin, but you also lost the benefit of cheap 5 percent money on the old 15,000,000. Thinking about the true marginal cost of the extra borrowing is the core of a refinance decision.

Say that out loud now.

A cash-out refinance only pays if the cash earns more than the cash flow I gave up, divided by the cash I took out.

Door two: sell

Sell at 30,000,000 dollars. Selling costs, such as brokerage, legal fees and any transfer tax, are a hypothetical 2 percent, 600,000 dollars; the actual level is commercial practice and local law. Repay the loan of 15,000,000 dollars. Before tax, you are left with 14,400,000 dollars. Tomorrow Elias will show that the tax on the gain may be large; for now, take a hypothetical tax of 2,300,000 dollars, chosen only for arithmetic. After-tax cash is 12,100,000 dollars.

Holding the building, that equity earned 700,000 dollars, which is about 5.8 percent on 12,100,000. Selling pays if you can redeploy 12,100,000 dollars at a better risk-adjusted return than 5.8 percent plus the growth you expected from the building. You also face reinvestment risk: the chance that you cannot quickly find something as good to buy, so the cash sits earning little while you search.

Door three: hold

Holding keeps 700,000 dollars of cash flow, the future NOI growth, the leverage at 50 percent and the full exposure to this one building and one market. It defers transaction costs and tax. The risk is that the return on equity in place is low, about 4.7 percent on 15,000,000 dollars before tax, and that the building's whole value rides on one market.

Comparing on one page

DoorCash nowAnnual cash flowDSCRLoan to value
Hold0700,0002.050 percent
Refinance2,700,000370,0001.3960 percent
Sell12,100,000 after hypothetical tax0nonenone

Read the table as risk as well as return. The refinance row is the only one where a 20 percent fall in NOI changes the picture badly: NOI of 1,200,000 dollars against debt service of 1,080,000 gives DSCR of 1.11, close to the level at which many loans hit a covenant. The hold row survives the same fall with DSCR of 1.6.

A second worked example: a partial refinance

The doors have dimmer switches. Suppose instead you refinance to 16,500,000 dollars at 5.5 percent, releasing about 1,250,000 dollars after 250,000 of costs. Debt service becomes 907,500 dollars and cash flow after reserves 542,500 dollars, down 157,500 from the hold case. The cash pays if it earns more than 157,500 divided by 1,250,000, which is 12.6 percent. Coverage is about 1.65, and a 20 percent fall in NOI leaves it at about 1.32, comfortably above most covenants. The smaller refinance releases less cash and costs about the same in marginal terms, but it keeps the building safe. Often the right answer is not whether to refinance, but how much.

The lender's view of each door

A lender reading your request asks three questions. Is the new loan sized to in-place NOI at today's rate, with coverage room? Where is the cash going: into another investment, into the building, or into the sponsor's pocket? And what is left in the building as equity cushion if values fall? A cash-out that distributes everything and leaves 40 percent equity at today's value may be acceptable; one that leaves 25 percent usually is not. Those are commercial practices of lenders, not rules, and they vary.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

Warrick here. On your personal balance sheet, a refinance does not create wealth; it converts equity into cash and adds a liability. Your net worth is unchanged on the day, less the costs. What changes is your liquidity and your risk. A sale converts an illiquid asset into liquid cash, which lowers concentration and raises flexibility but usually triggers tax. Record each door in three lines: net worth after costs and tax, liquid assets, and the share of net worth in this one building. A licensed adviser is required before you act on a personal decision this informs.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a cash-out refinance that looks free because the cash is not taxed, while it quietly cuts cash flow and coverage until a modest fall in NOI threatens the loan. The control is to price the marginal cost of the extra borrowing and stress the new DSCR for a fall in NOI before signing.

The beginner's mistake

Comparing doors before tax. A sale and a refinance can look similar pre-tax and differ by millions after it. Tomorrow's lesson is where the comparison becomes honest.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman built stress tests: base, downside and severe cases, break-evens and triggers. Each door in today's table deserves the same treatment. A decision that only works in the base case is not a decision; it is a hope.

Recap

Refinancing swaps cash flow and safety for cash now, and pays only if the cash beats the marginal cost of the extra debt. Selling swaps growth for certainty, at the cost of selling expenses, tax and reinvestment risk. Holding keeps growth and concentration. Stress every door for a fall in NOI.

Next: Elias on The Rules: the tax and contract rules behind each door, and Two Systems.
checklist: I price the marginal cost of extra borrowing, not just the new rate.
I calculate the cash-out amount after fees and any prepayment penalty.
I stress the new DSCR for a 20 percent fall in NOI.
I compare redeployment returns with the cash flow each door gives up.
I allow for reinvestment risk when I sell.
I compare doors after tax, never only before.
I record net worth, liquidity and concentration for each door.
head: Field checklist
speak: Each door trades one thing for another. In my hypothetical base case, a building earns 1,500,000 dollars of NOI, is worth 30,000,000 and owes 15,000,000 at 5 percent, so cash flow is 700,000 and coverage is 2.0. A cash-out refinance to 18,000,000 at 6 percent releases 2,700,000 dollars but cuts cash flow to 370,000 and coverage to about 1.39. That pays only if the cash earns more than about 12 percent, because I gave up 330,000 a year to get it. Selling, after costs and a hypothetical tax, leaves about 12,100,000 dollars, which must beat the building's 5.8 percent plus its growth, and I carry reinvestment risk while I look. Holding keeps growth and risk. I stress every door for a 20 percent fall in NOI, and I never compare doors before tax.
terms: Prepayment penalty — a charge set by the loan agreement for repaying a loan before its maturity.
Cash-out refinance — replacing a loan with a larger one and taking the difference, after costs, as cash.
Reinvestment risk — the risk that money released by a sale cannot quickly be invested at a comparable return.

hostile.q: You want to refinance to 60 percent and take 2,700,000 dollars out. What happens to my loan if NOI falls 20 percent?
hostile.a: Coverage falls from about 1.39 to about 1.11, which is close to your covenant, so I do not want you to rely on my optimism. I will show you the stress at 10, 20 and 30 percent, the reserve I will hold back from the proceeds against that case, and the cash management trigger I am willing to accept. If the numbers do not satisfy your credit committee at 20 percent, I would rather take a smaller loan.

title: The Rules Behind the Doors: Realisation, Recapture and the Clauses That Decide Timing
summary: Tax law usually treats a sale very differently from a loan, and contract terms in loans and partner agreements often decide when you can act. This lesson teaches realisation, the capital-versus-income question, recapture of depreciation and the trap of debt above tax cost, then compares Canada and Guyana conceptually.
body:
Tax law usually taxes what you realise, not what you borrow, and contracts usually decide when you are allowed to realise. Understand both and the after-tax comparison of hold, sell and refinance becomes honest.

Recall

Q. What is a prepayment penalty?

A. A charge set by the loan agreement for repaying a loan before maturity.

Q. Why can a 15 percent value gain overstate what management achieved?

A. Because part of it may come from a falling cap rate, which is the market, or from cutting reserves, which only moves cost to later.

Q. What is the difference between avoidance and evasion?

A. Evasion is illegal concealment or misrepresentation. Avoidance is arranging affairs within the law to reduce tax, but anti-avoidance rules can deny a benefit where an arrangement lacks substance or abuses the purpose of the law.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the difference between a sale and a refinance is often larger in tax than in anything else. I teach concepts only. Rates, inclusion rules, holding periods and reliefs vary by jurisdiction and change. Verify every rule against the primary source before you rely on it. Professional sign-off required: tax adviser in each jurisdiction involved, before any sale, refinance or restructuring.

Realisation: the event that wakes the tax

In plain English: in most systems, an increase in value is not taxed while you hold the asset. It is taxed when something happens that realises it, usually a sale.

The professional framing is the realisation principle. A disposition, which may include a sale, an exchange, a transfer to a related party or, in some systems, a deemed disposition on emigration or death, triggers the calculation of a gain: proceeds less the tax cost of the asset and the costs of sale. A loan, by contrast, is generally not income, because you owe it back. That is why a refinance usually does not create a tax event while a sale does. There are exceptions and anti-avoidance rules, so this is a concept, not a conclusion.

Capital or income: the first question on any gain

Before you calculate, ask what kind of gain it is. A gain on an investment held for the long term is commonly treated as a capital gain. A gain on property bought or built to sell, which is the developer's trade, may be treated as business income, often at a less favourable treatment. The test usually looks at intention at acquisition, the length of ownership, the frequency of similar transactions and how the asset was used. A developer who builds to hold and later sells may find the authorities asking whether the intention was always to sell. Records made at the time, such as a business plan showing a long hold and board minutes, are evidence of intention.

Recapture: the depreciation comes back

Many systems let an owner deduct depreciation, a tax allowance for the wear of a building, against rental income each year. That deduction lowers the tax cost of the building. On sale, the deductions previously claimed may be recaptured, meaning taxed back, often as ordinary income rather than as a capital gain.

A worked example with hypothetical round numbers and a hypothetical rate used only for arithmetic. A building cost 20,000,000 dollars. Over the years, 3,000,000 dollars of depreciation was deducted, so the tax cost is now 17,000,000 dollars. It sells for 30,000,000 dollars with 600,000 dollars of selling costs. The total gain is 30,000,000 minus 600,000 minus 17,000,000, which is 12,400,000 dollars. Of that, 3,000,000 dollars may be recapture and 9,400,000 dollars a capital gain. If, hypothetically, recapture were taxed at 30 percent and the capital gain at 20 percent, the tax would be 900,000 plus 1,880,000, which is 2,780,000 dollars. The actual rates and categories in your jurisdiction will differ.

Say that out loud now.

The depreciation I deducted while holding may be taxed back when I sell. It was a deferral, not a gift.

The trap: debt above tax cost

Here is the trap that refinancing sets. Suppose you cash-out refinance repeatedly, until the loan is 25,000,000 dollars against a tax cost of 17,000,000 dollars. You then sell for 26,000,000 dollars. After costs of 520,000 dollars and repaying the loan, you receive about 480,000 dollars of cash. But the gain is 26,000,000 minus 520,000 minus 17,000,000, about 8,480,000 dollars, and the tax on it, at any meaningful rate, may exceed the cash you received. The tax was always waiting; the refinances spent the cash that should have paid it. Some advisers call that the negative equity trap. Before any cash-out, estimate the tax that a later sale would trigger and keep the loan below the point at which the sale stops paying it.

Deferral routes and their price

Some systems offer routes that defer tax on a sale if proceeds are reinvested in similar property within set periods, or if property moves between related entities on a rollover basis. These are technical, condition-heavy and easy to lose on a missed deadline or a cash payment taken at the wrong moment. Treat any deferral route as a project with a tax adviser in charge, not a box ticked at closing.

The contract rules that decide timing

Three clause families decide when you may use a door. In the loan: prepayment terms, lockout periods during which repayment is not allowed, and due-on-sale clauses that make the loan payable if the property is sold. In partner agreements: major-decision consents for a sale or new debt, rights of first offer or refusal that let a partner buy first, and buy-sell provisions. In leases: tenants' rights of first refusal, which in some places are also set by statute. Read all three before you plan a date.

A short example. A loan carries a lockout for the first three years and a prepayment charge after that. Your hold analysis says sell in year two. Unless the buyer can assume the loan, which needs the lender's consent, the lockout may make a sale before year three impossible or very costly. The analysis was right and the timing was not available. That is why the contract review comes before the spreadsheet is finalised.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source. In Canada, as a concept, capital gains are taxed within the income tax system, with only a portion of the gain included in income, and the allowance for depreciation, called capital cost allowance, can be recaptured as income on sale; the inclusion portion and the rules have changed over time and are subject to debate. In Guyana, as a concept, capital gains are addressed through a separate capital gains statute distinct from the income tax on business profits, and property transfers can also attract separate duties. In both, the capital-versus-income question decides which regime applies. Rates, holding periods, exemptions and inclusion rules must be confirmed in the current law of each country [unverified — confirm independently].

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is planning a sale or refinance on pre-tax numbers, then discovering recapture, income characterisation or a tax larger than the cash proceeds. The control is an after-tax estimate prepared with a tax adviser before any decision, updated every time the loan or the plan changes.

The beginner's mistake

Treating refinance cash as free money. It is untaxed when received in many systems because it is owed back, and the tax on the underlying gain is still waiting for the sale.

Callback

In Week 64, Elias and Omar taught exit tax: asset versus share sale, recapture and departure tax concepts. Today's lesson applies the same ideas to a single building. The exit is designed long before it happens, every time you claim depreciation or take cash out.

Recap

Tax usually follows realisation, so a sale triggers it and a loan usually does not. Ask first whether a gain is capital or income. Depreciation claimed may be recaptured. Debt above tax cost can make sale tax exceed sale cash. Loan, partner and lease clauses decide timing.

Next: Sage on The Numbers: an after-tax comparison of all three doors, step by step.
checklist: I ask whether a gain would be capital or income before I estimate tax.
I keep records made at the time that show my intention when I acquired the asset.
I know the tax cost of each building and the depreciation claimed to date.
I estimate recapture before any sale.
I check that no cash-out refinance pushes debt toward the point where sale tax exceeds sale cash.
I read prepayment, lockout and due-on-sale clauses before choosing a date.
I read partner consents, rights of first offer and buy-sell terms before planning a sale.
I treat any deferral route as an adviser-led project.
head: Field checklist
speak: Tax usually follows realisation. A sale is a disposition that triggers a gain: proceeds, less tax cost, less selling costs. A loan generally is not income because I owe it back, which is why a refinance usually creates no tax on the day. The first question on any gain is whether it is capital or business income; intention at acquisition, length of hold and frequency of sales decide it, so records made at the time matter. Depreciation I deducted while holding lowers my tax cost and may be recaptured when I sell. And repeated cash-out refinances can push debt above tax cost, until a sale produces more tax than cash. Contracts decide timing too: prepayment and lockout terms, due-on-sale clauses, partner consents and rights of first offer. I teach concepts, not conclusions. Every rate and rule is verified against the primary source, with a tax adviser in each jurisdiction.
terms: Realisation — the event, usually a sale or other disposition, that causes an increase in value to be measured and taxed.
Recapture — the taxing back, on sale, of depreciation deductions previously claimed against income.
Tax cost — the amount the tax system recognises as invested in an asset, typically purchase cost plus improvements, less depreciation claimed.

hostile.q: You have taken three cash-out refinances. What is your tax cost, and what would a sale today leave you after tax?
hostile.a: The tax cost is on the schedule I keep for each building: original cost, improvements, depreciation claimed and the resulting figure, prepared with my accountant. I have an adviser's estimate of the tax a sale would trigger, including recapture, and the net cash after loan repayment and costs. It is positive, and I have a rule not to refinance past the point where it would not be. I can share the schedule.

title: The After-Tax Comparison: Three Doors, One Spreadsheet
summary: A worked, step-by-step comparison of holding, selling and refinancing one hypothetical building over five years, after costs and a hypothetical tax, ending in the wealth each door leaves and the return each produces on equity in place.
body:
The only fair comparison of hold, sell and refinance is the wealth each leaves you at the same future date, after costs and tax. Build it once, step by step, and you will never again compare doors on a feeling.

Recall

Q. What is recapture?

A. The taxing back, on sale, of depreciation deductions previously claimed against income.

Q. What is a variance threshold in investor reporting?

A. An agreed level of difference from budget above which the manager reports to investors in writing before the regular report.

Q. What does functional testing prove at closeout?

A. That each system operates as designed under its normal modes, before integrated testing proves that systems work correctly together.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the calculation that decides whether your largest asset stays, goes or is borrowed against. Every number here is hypothetical, including the tax rates, which are chosen for arithmetic and are not any jurisdiction's rates. The method is what you keep.

Step 1: the facts

Value today: 30,000,000 dollars. NOI: 1,500,000 dollars, expected to grow 2 percent a year. Loan: 15,000,000 dollars at 5 percent interest only, maturing in five years. Reserve: 50,000 dollars a year. Tax cost: 17,000,000 dollars, of which 3,000,000 dollars is depreciation already claimed. Selling costs: 2 percent of price. Hypothetical tax: recapture at 30 percent, capital gain at 20 percent, and tax on annual cash flow at 25 percent, ignoring further depreciation for simplicity. Exit cap rate in five years: 5 percent. Alternative investment for released cash: 7 percent before tax, taxed at 25 percent, so 5.25 percent after tax.

Step 2: sell today

Price 30,000,000. Selling costs 600,000. Gain: 30,000,000 minus 600,000 minus 17,000,000, which is 12,400,000 dollars, of which 3,000,000 is recapture and 9,400,000 is capital gain. Tax: 900,000 plus 1,880,000, which is 2,780,000 dollars. Cash after loan and tax: 30,000,000 minus 600,000 minus 15,000,000 minus 2,780,000, which is 11,620,000 dollars.

Invest it at 5.25 percent after tax for five years. Compounding annually, 11,620,000 times 1.0525 to the fifth power is about 15,010,000 dollars. Wealth at year five if you sell today: about 15,010,000 dollars, in cash.

Step 3: hold for five years, then sell

NOI grows 2 percent a year: about 1,530,000, 1,561,000, 1,592,000, 1,624,000 and 1,656,000 dollars. Each year, cash flow is NOI less 750,000 dollars of interest and 50,000 of reserve. Year one cash flow is about 730,000; year five about 856,000. After tax at 25 percent, the five years total roughly 3,000,000 dollars. Reinvested at 5.25 percent after tax as received, they reach about 3,290,000 dollars by year five.

At year five, value is year-six NOI, about 1,689,000 dollars, divided by 0.05, which is about 33,780,000 dollars. Selling costs about 676,000. Gain: 33,780,000 minus 676,000 minus 17,000,000, which is about 16,109,000 dollars, of which 3,000,000 is recapture and 13,109,000 capital gain. Tax: 900,000 plus 2,622,000, about 3,522,000 dollars. Cash after loan and tax: 33,780,000 minus 676,000 minus 15,000,000 minus 3,522,000, about 14,587,000 dollars. Add the reinvested cash flow, and wealth at year five is about 17,870,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Compare doors at the same future date, after costs and after tax. Anything else is comparing a photograph with a film.

Step 4: refinance today, hold five years, then sell

Refinance to 18,000,000 dollars at 6 percent, with 300,000 dollars of costs, releasing 2,700,000 dollars, assumed untaxed when received; verify that concept against the primary source. Invest it at 5.25 percent after tax: about 3,490,000 dollars by year five.

Annual interest is now 1,080,000 dollars. Year one cash flow: 1,530,000 minus 1,080,000 minus 50,000, which is 400,000; year five about 526,000. After tax at 25 percent, about 1,730,000 dollars in total, reinvested to about 1,910,000. For simplicity, treat the 300,000 dollars of refinancing costs as having no tax effect in this example, though in real life they may be deductible over time.

At year five, sell at 33,780,000. Costs 676,000. The gain is the same 16,109,000 and the tax the same 3,522,000, because borrowing did not change the tax cost. Cash after the larger loan and tax: 33,780,000 minus 676,000 minus 18,000,000 minus 3,522,000, which is about 11,587,000 dollars. Total wealth at year five: 11,587,000 plus 3,490,000 plus 1,910,000, about 17,000,000 dollars.

Step 5: read the result

DoorWealth at year five, hypothetical
Sell todayabout 15,010,000
Hold, then sellabout 17,870,000
Refinance, hold, then sellabout 17,000,000

Here, holding wins because the building's return, with cheap existing debt and deferred tax, beats the 5.25 percent alternative. The refinance loses about 880,000 dollars against holding, because it swapped 5 percent debt for 6 percent debt on the whole balance and invested the cash at only 5.25 percent after tax. Raise the alternative return to 10 percent after tax, and the sell-today figure becomes about 18,710,000 dollars, beating both. The answer depends most on the alternative return, which is the number you least control. Run the table at several alternatives before deciding.

Find the break-even. Solve for the after-tax alternative return at which selling today equals holding. Selling today must grow 11,620,000 dollars to about 17,870,000 in five years, a factor of about 1.538. The fifth root of 1.538 is about 1.090, so the break-even is about 9 percent after tax. That single number is the most useful line in the analysis. If you honestly believe you can redeploy the equity at more than 9 percent after tax, at similar risk, selling wins; if not, holding wins. Put that sentence in the memo.

Step 6: add risk

The table is a base case. Stress it: exit cap rate at 6 percent instead of 5, and the year-five value falls to about 28,150,000 dollars, cutting the hold result by more than 4,000,000 dollars and the refinance result by the same, while the sell-today figure is untouched. That is the price of certainty, and the reason the cycle matters.

Step 7: what the table leaves out

Three things never fit neatly in the table and must be written beside it. Concentration: if this building is most of your net worth, selling has a value the arithmetic does not capture. Effort: holding requires asset management for five more years, and your time has an alternative too. And the estate: in some systems, the tax treatment of an asset held until death differs from one sold during life, which can change the hold result materially. Name each one in a sentence, so that the decision maker weighs them deliberately rather than forgetting them.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is comparing doors at different times or before tax, which almost always flatters holding or refinancing. The control is a single table at one future date, after costs and tax, run at several alternative returns and exit cap rates.

The beginner's mistake

Leaving out the tax on the sale at the end of the hold. Holding defers tax; it does not remove it, unless a specific relief applies, which is a matter for an adviser.

A second mistake is reinvesting the hold case's interim cash flow at one rate and the sale proceeds at another. Every dollar released by any door should grow at the same after-tax alternative return, or the comparison is rigged before it starts. If you believe your best alternative changes over time, change it for every door at once.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage and Elias taught levered and unlevered IRR, the equity multiple and after-tax leakage. This lesson is that toolkit used at the decision that matters most: comparing three futures at the same date, with every leak counted.

Recap

Compute the wealth each door leaves at the same future date, after selling costs and tax. Selling today is certain but pays cost and tax early. Holding defers both. Refinancing adds cash and cost. The alternative return and the exit cap rate decide the winner, so run several.

Next: JAX on The Room: the partner meeting when one investor wants to sell and you want to hold.
checklist: I state every assumption, including hypothetical tax rates, at the top of the analysis.
I compare all doors at the same future date.
I include selling costs and tax on the final sale in every hold case.
I reinvest interim cash flow at the same after-tax alternative rate across doors.
I remember that borrowing does not change the tax cost of the asset.
I run the table at several alternative returns.
I stress the exit cap rate before choosing to hold.
head: Field checklist
speak: To compare hold, sell and refinance honestly, I calculate the wealth each leaves at the same future date, after costs and tax. In my hypothetical case, selling today leaves about 11,620,000 dollars after loan and tax, which grows to about 15,010,000 by year five at 5.25 percent after tax. Holding five years and then selling leaves about 17,870,000, because the building's return on cheap existing debt, with tax deferred, beats the alternative. Refinancing today, holding and then selling leaves about 17,000,000, because it replaced 5 percent debt with 6 percent debt on the whole balance and invested the cash at only 5.25 percent. Borrowing does not change the tax cost, so the final sale tax is the same. The winner depends most on the alternative return and the exit cap rate. At a 10 percent alternative, selling today wins. So I run the table several ways before I decide.
terms: Common future date — the single point in time at which competing options are compared, so that time differences do not distort the result.
Alternative return — the after-tax return the released equity could earn in its next best use at similar risk.
Exit cap rate — the capitalisation rate assumed for the sale at the end of a hold period.

hostile.q: Your hold case beats selling by almost 3,000,000 dollars. What exit cap rate does that assume, and what if it is a point higher?
hostile.a: It assumes 5 percent, the same as today. At 6 percent, year-five value falls to about 28,150,000 dollars and the hold result drops by more than 4,000,000, which puts it below selling today. So the hold case is a bet that cap rates do not rise by much in five years. I have the table at 5, 5.5 and 6 percent, and my recommendation names the cap rate at which I would sell instead.

title: When Your Partner Wants to Sell and You Want to Hold
summary: A realistic scene: an investor partner who wants to sell into a strong market meets a developer who wants to hold. Learn the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent and how to hold your state. A monthly thread on working with advisers closes the lesson.
body:
When partners disagree about selling, the argument is rarely about the building. It is about two different balance sheets, time horizons and tax positions. Find those differences and the deal usually solves itself.

Recall

Q. Why must hold, sell and refinance be compared at the same future date?

A. Because cash today and wealth in five years are not comparable unless the released cash is grown at an alternative return to the same date, after tax.

Q. What is a right of first offer in a partner agreement?

A. A right for a partner to make the first offer to buy an interest or the property before it is offered to outsiders. Its exact mechanics are set by the agreement.

Q. What is a capital needs assessment?

A. An engineer's schedule of each building component, its remaining life and replacement cost, used to size a capital reserve.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a joint venture that works brilliantly during construction can fracture at the first strong offer. Your investor partner may need liquidity, may face a different tax result, or may have promised its own investors a return by a date. If you treat the disagreement as a test of who is right about the market, you will win the argument and lose the partner. This scene is practice for the first time it happens.

The scene

A hypothetical building you developed with one investor partner who holds 80 percent of the equity; you hold 20 percent and manage it. An unsolicited offer has arrived at a price that implies a 4.5 percent cap rate on current NOI, attractive by any measure. Your partner's representative says, "We should take it." Your own hold analysis says that, with cheap existing debt and deferred tax, holding beats selling at your alternative return. The agreement requires both partners to consent to a sale, and gives either partner a right of first offer on the other's interest.

The question behind the question

"We should take it" can mean several things, and each has a different answer. It may mean: our fund must return capital to its own investors by a date. It may mean: our tax result on a sale is better than yours. It may mean: we think the market has peaked. Or it may mean: we have lost confidence in the business plan. Ask, before arguing: "Help me understand what selling does for you that holding does not." Then listen to the whole answer.

The lines to say

"I agree the price is strong. Let me show you how I compared it." Put the one-page comparison on the table: wealth at year five for each door, at several alternative returns and exit cap rates, with the cap rate at which you would sell named. Then: "If your fund needs liquidity by a date, there may be a way for you to get it without either of us selling the whole building."

That last line opens the doors in between. You could exercise your right of first offer and buy some or all of the partner's interest, financed by a new equity partner or a refinance. The partner could sell its interest to a new investor at a price based on the offer. Or both of you could sell a minority stake, releasing cash to the partner while you keep management.

Say that out loud now.

What does selling do for you that holding does not?

The lines never to say

"You don't understand this market." It insults the partner and invites them to prove you wrong with their consent right. "I won't agree to a sale." A flat refusal turns a consent right into a deadlock, and deadlock clauses tend to end in forced sales that suit nobody. "Trust me, it will be worth more in five years." Without the table, that is a sales line, not an analysis.

When to stay silent

After you ask the question behind the question, stop and let the answer come out in full, including the part the partner did not plan to say. After you show the table, stay silent while they read it. The silence is them doing your arithmetic; let them do it.

Holding your state

You may feel this as a challenge to your judgement or to the building you made. Name that privately, then set it aside; the building's value does not depend on who wins the meeting. If you notice your voice speeding up, slow it deliberately and lower it slightly. Before the meeting, seated and never while driving, a few slow breaths with a long out-breath is a practitioner habit some people find steadying; check with your doctor if you have any condition that makes breathing exercises unsuitable.

A worked example of the bridge

Hypothetical numbers. The offer is 33,000,000 dollars on a building owing 15,000,000. Net of 2 percent costs, equity is 17,340,000 dollars, of which the partner's 80 percent is 13,872,000 before tax. You propose to buy half the partner's interest, 40 percent of the equity, at the same implied price, about 6,936,000 dollars, funded by a new equity partner who has agreed terms in principle. The original partner receives cash for half its position at the market price and keeps 40 percent; you keep management and a growing building. Professional sign-off required: lawyer on the transfer and consent mechanics, and tax advisers for each partner, because a partial sale has its own tax consequences.

Working with advisers

A monthly thread. Your partner's position on a sale will usually be set by its advisers before it reaches you, so when the position seems unreasonable, ask whether its tax adviser or fund counsel has seen your analysis. Offer to have your adviser speak to theirs. Advisers who talk directly often find solutions that principals, defending positions, cannot.

Be equally clear with your own advisers about what you want from them: not permission, but the consequences of each door, in writing, with the assumptions named. Ask each one, "What would make you change this advice?" The answer tells you which assumption to watch.

What to write after the meeting

Within two working days, send a short note: the offer and its implied cap rate, each door's same-date result, the constraint your partner named, the structure you proposed, what each side will now do and by when. A partner who sees its own constraint written accurately in your words is far more likely to trust your proposed structure, and the note becomes the record if the agreement's deadlock clause is ever reached.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is turning a disagreement about timing into a deadlock, which hands the outcome to a clause rather than to the partners. The control is to find the partner's real constraint first, then offer a structure, such as a partial buyout, that meets it.

The beginner's mistake

Arguing about the market. Neither of you can prove where cap rates will be in five years. You can both agree on what each partner needs.

The second beginner's mistake is treating the partner's first answer as its final one. "We need the money" may become, after a question or two, "we need to show our own investors a realised return this year." Those are different problems. The first needs cash; the second may be solved by a partial sale that crystallises a return on part of the position. Keep asking until the constraint is specific enough to design around.

Callback

In Week 69, JAX and LEX taught partner agreements: deadlock, drag and tag, buy-sell provisions and rights of first offer. Those clauses were written for exactly this meeting. Read them before the meeting, so you know what happens if you cannot agree, and so that you never have to find out.

Recap

A sale dispute is usually about different partners' constraints, not the building. Ask what selling does for them that holding does not. Show the analysis, avoid flat refusals, and offer the doors in between, such as a partial buyout. Stay silent while they read. Let advisers talk to advisers.

Next: Kema on the week's quiz and recap, with a Red Pen drill on a flawed hold memo.
checklist: I ask what selling does for my partner that holding does not, before arguing.
I bring a one-page, after-tax comparison of the doors to the meeting.
I know the consent, deadlock and right-of-first-offer clauses before I walk in.
I offer a structure in between, such as a partial buyout, when constraints differ.
I never refuse flatly or argue about where the market will go.
I stay silent while my partner reads the analysis.
I offer to let our advisers speak directly.
head: Field checklist
speak: When my partner wants to sell and I want to hold, the disagreement is usually about our different situations, not the building. My partner may need liquidity by a date, may face a different tax result, or may have lost confidence in the plan. So before arguing, I ask: what does selling do for you that holding does not? Then I listen to the whole answer. I bring a one-page after-tax comparison of the doors and name the cap rate at which I would sell. I never say they do not understand the market, and I never refuse flatly, because a refusal turns a consent right into a deadlock. Instead I offer the doors in between: I buy part of their interest using my right of first offer, they sell to a new investor at the market price, or we sell a minority stake together. And I let our advisers talk directly.
terms: Consent right — a partner's contractual right to approve or block a major decision, such as a sale or new debt.
Partial buyout — the purchase by one partner, or a new investor, of part of another partner's interest.
Deadlock — a state in which partners with equal or blocking rights cannot agree, often resolved by a clause in the agreement.

hostile.q: We own 80 percent and want our capital back. Why should we let you keep our money in this building?
hostile.a: You should not have to, if you need it back. I am not asking you to stay; I am asking you not to sell the whole building to get your capital, because my analysis shows that costs us both value. I can arrange for half your interest to be bought now at the offer's implied price, and the remainder at the same formula within a set period, so you get liquidity at market value and the building is not sold below what it is worth to a long holder.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 127 Review: Equity in Place, Three Doors and the Tax That Waits
summary: Six questions test the week's ideas on hold, sell and refinance. A Red Pen drill finds the planted defects in a hypothetical hold memo. A two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one question asked every year: should the equity now in this building stay there, measured at the same future date, after costs, after tax and after risk?

Recall

Q. What should you ask first when a partner wants to sell and you want to hold?

A. What selling does for them that holding does not. The answer usually reveals a constraint that a structure can meet.

Q. What wins a property tax appeal?

A. Filing within the window, and evidence of value on the valuation date: reconciled statements, the rent roll, comparable sales and an independent appraisal.

Q. What is the difference between a warranty and a latent defect claim?

A. A warranty is a promise in the contract to repair defects that appear within a stated period. A latent defect claim concerns defects that could not reasonably be found at completion, and its limits depend on the contract and the law.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the decision you will make most often as an owner, and the one most often made by default. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What is return on equity in place, and why does success lower it?

Answer: Annual cash flow after debt and reserves divided by the equity you could take out today after debt, costs and tax. Success raises value faster than income, so the same cash flow is spread over more equity.

Question 2. When does a cash-out refinance pay?

Answer: When the cash released earns more than the cash flow given up divided by the cash taken out, and the building can carry the higher debt service through a fall in NOI.

Question 3. Why does a sale usually trigger tax and a refinance usually does not?

Answer: Tax usually follows realisation; a sale is a disposition, and a loan is owed back, so it is not income. Verify the rule in each jurisdiction against the primary source.

Question 4. What is the trap of debt above tax cost?

Answer: After repeated cash-out refinances, a sale can produce tax on the gain that exceeds the cash left after repaying the loan.

Question 5. How do you compare the three doors fairly?

Answer: Calculate the wealth each leaves at the same future date, after selling costs and tax, with interim cash reinvested at the same after-tax alternative, and run it at several alternatives and exit cap rates.

Question 6. State Rule 127.

Answer: Never let the debt decide your hold; match loan term to the time the asset needs, ladder maturities, stress-test every refinance and start at least eighteen months before maturity.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Sage and Elias framed hold, sell and refinance as one question about equity in place. Ford and Roman took Olympia and York, long buildings on short money, giving Rule 127. Roman priced what each door does to cash, coverage and leverage. Elias taught realisation, capital versus income, recapture and the debt-above-cost trap, with Two Systems. Sage built the after-tax comparison at one future date. JAX ran the partner meeting.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical extract from an owner's hold memo and find the defects before reading on.

Hold Recommendation, Building A. We recommend holding. Our equity has earned 12 percent a year on the 6,000,000 dollars originally invested, well above alternatives. A refinance to 70 percent loan to value would release 5,000,000 dollars tax free, which we would distribute. The loan matures in 9 months; we will refinance at that time. The building should be worth 36,000,000 dollars in five years. Selling today would cost us selling fees and tax, so holding is clearly better.

The defects. First, return is measured on the original equity, not the equity in place, which flatters the hold. Second, "tax free" refinance cash is untaxed when received in many systems but does not remove the tax waiting on sale, and the memo never checks whether debt would exceed tax cost. Third, distributing all the cash out leaves no reserve against the higher debt service, and no DSCR stress is shown. Fourth, a maturity 9 months away with refinancing left until "that time" breaks Rule 127. Fifth, the 36,000,000 dollar future value has no stated NOI growth or exit cap rate. Sixth, the comparison counts the costs and tax of selling today but not the costs and tax of selling later, so the doors are not compared at the same date after tax.

The boardroom drill

Stand up and explain this week in two minutes. Then compare with the model answer.

Model answer: "Every year we ask whether the equity in each building should stay there. We measure return on equity in place, which is cash flow divided by what we could take out today after debt, costs and tax, not on what we originally invested. There are three doors. Holding keeps growth and risk and defers tax. Selling pays costs and tax for cash to redeploy. Refinancing releases cash, usually untaxed when received, but raises debt service and leaves the sale tax waiting. We compare them by the wealth each leaves at the same date after tax, at several alternative returns and exit cap rates. We never let debt maturity make the decision for us: we ladder maturities and start refinancing eighteen months early. When partners disagree, we find their constraint and solve it with a structure."

Score yourself: equity in place defined, all three doors named with their trade, same-date after-tax comparison, Rule 127, under two minutes.

How to use this review

Mark any answer you gave slowly or with the wrong concept, return to that day's lesson and read only the section that answers it, then answer again tomorrow aloud. This week, the two questions that matter most are Question 2 and Question 5, because they protect you from the two most expensive mistakes: a refinance that quietly weakens the building, and a comparison that flatters the option you already preferred.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a memo that compares doors on original equity, before tax and at different dates, and so recommends whatever its author already believed. The control is the same-date after-tax table, with stresses.

The beginner's mistake

Calling refinance cash tax free and stopping there. Ask what the sale will owe when it comes.

The second mistake is treating the Red Pen as an exercise in finding errors of arithmetic. Of the six defects in this memo, not one is a wrong sum. Each is a wrong base, a missing cost, an untested assumption or a date left too late. Real memos fail the same way, which is why the habit of reading for structure matters more than checking the maths.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the pre-mortem: imagine the decision has failed and ask why. Apply it to a hold recommendation: it is five years from now and holding was the wrong call. The usual answers are a higher exit cap rate, a maturity in a bad market and a better use of the equity, which is exactly what this week's table tests.

Run one more pre-mortem on the other doors. It is five years from now and selling was the wrong call: the usual reasons are that the cash sat idle, the replacement deal was worse, and tax paid early was never earned back. It is five years from now and the refinance was wrong: NOI dipped, coverage fell near the covenant and the cash had already been distributed. Each door has its own typical failure. Naming them in advance is what turns the table into a decision.

Recap

Measure return on equity in place. Price what each door gives and takes. Count tax on every sale, now and later. Compare at one future date. Ladder maturities and start early. Solve partner disagreements by finding constraints.

checklist: What is return on equity in place, and why does success lower it?
When does a cash-out refinance pay?
Why does a sale usually trigger tax and a refinance usually does not?
What is the trap of debt above tax cost?
How do you compare the three doors fairly?
State Rule 127.
head: The six questions
speak: This week I learned that hold, sell and refinance are one question: should the equity in place stay? I measure return on equity in place, cash flow over what I could take out today after debt, costs and tax, because success lowers that return even while the original-equity return looks great. Holding keeps growth and risk and defers tax. Selling pays costs and tax for cash. Refinancing releases cash, usually untaxed when received because it is owed back, but raises debt service and leaves the sale tax waiting; repeated refinances can push debt above tax cost until a sale produces more tax than cash. I compare all three by the wealth each leaves at the same future date after tax, at several alternative returns and exit cap rates. Rule 127: never let the debt decide my hold. And when a partner wants to sell, I find their constraint first.
terms: Equity in place — market value less debt, selling costs and, for comparison, the tax a sale would trigger.
Same-date comparison — comparing options by the wealth each leaves at one future date, after costs and tax.
Refinance gap — the shortfall between a maturing loan's balance and the largest new loan the building's income will support.

hostile.q: Your memo says hold because equity earned 12 percent. Twelve percent on what?
hostile.a: On the original 6,000,000 dollars, which is the wrong base, and I will restate it. On equity in place after debt, costs and the tax a sale would trigger, the return is much lower. I will bring a same-date comparison of all three doors after tax, with the loan maturity addressed now rather than in nine months, and I will make the recommendation on that table, whichever door it favours.
